featured.title: Historical Intersections of Climatic Change and Power Transitions: Ecological Pressure, Differential Adaptability, and the U.S.-China Power Transition in the Anthropocene
featured.summary: Accepted and DOI-registered but not yet released (the DOI resolves to Crossref's 'pending publication' page as of August 2026), so no abstract is yet public. On the evidence of the title and the authors' own listing, the paper argues that climatic change and power transitions have historically intersected: ecological pressure does not affect all contenders equally but redistributes relative power according to states' differential capacity to adapt, and the authors extend this historical mechanism to the U.S.-China power transition under Anthropocene conditions.

featured.title: Historical Intersections of Climatic Change and Power Transitions: Ecological Pressure, Balance of Adaptability, and the U.S.-China Power Transition in the Anthropocene
featured.venue: International Relations of the Asia-Pacific (Oxford University Press)
featured.summary: Co-authored with Inho Choi, this article brings climatic change into power-transition theory by arguing that ecological pressure is a recurring driver of transition outcomes and that what determines who prevails is not raw material capability but a 'balance of adaptability' — the relative capacity of rival orders to absorb and reorganize under environmental stress. The authors read historical cases of climate-stressed transitions forward to the contemporary U.S.-China case in the Anthropocene. Listed as forthcoming on Oh's July 2026 CV; his March 2026 CV recorded it at Revise & Resubmit, so the acceptance is recent and no volume/DOI has been assigned yet.

featured.title: All but the Death Penalty: Incomplete Protection for Civilian Internee Mothers
featured.summary: Argues that unrecognized gender bias is built into the codification of international humanitarian law itself. Focusing on Article 76(3) of the 1977 Additional Protocol I, which forbids executing pregnant women and mothers of dependent children who are interned but still permits the death sentence to be pronounced against them, Kwon draws on the theory of benevolent sexism to contend that this 'preferential protection' encodes an essentialist picture of women as weak protectees by default. She further argues such benevolent protection predictably lapses once it collides with state interests in retaining discretion over women whose conduct exceeds traditional gender roles.

featured.title: Mandates through the Rule of Law: United Nations Missions and Foreign Direct Investment
featured.summary: Examines how the content of United Nations mission mandates -- specifically their rule-of-law components -- shapes foreign direct investment into host states, arguing that peace operations affect investor behaviour through the legal-institutional provisions they carry rather than through the mere presence of peacekeepers. CAUTION: no abstract was retrievable from CrossRef, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, or the publisher (ScienceDirect blocks automated access), so this summary is inferred from the published title and the author's own framing on her research page; the direction of the reported findings is NOT confirmed and should be checked against the article before quoting.

themes.title: Interpolity Orders and Their Organizing Principles
themes.blurb: Reconstructs orders that were not systems of sovereign states — the Ming–Chosŏn ritual order, Warring States tianxia, the inter-imperial Europe from which Franco's Spain had been disengaged — and asks what actually held each together: virtue, status, ritual reciprocity, imperial identity. The cluster is where the collective builds general theory (aretocracy, the virtue of state, status ascent, symbiotic statehood) out of non-European historical material rather than measuring that material against Westphalia.

entries.title: Non-Western Interpolity Orders and Sociocultural Forces: the shi in the Early Modern East Asian Order
entries.venue: The Chinese Journal of International Politics
entries.summary: Argues against the state-centric premise that empires and states alone make international order: transnational sociocultural forces did so too. From the Song period the literati (shi) of China, Korea and Vietnam became a transnational class increasingly autonomous from the state, producing what Choi calls a 'symbiotic form of state'; the shi then shaped the East Asian order both by steering the foreign-policy orientations of those symbiotic states and by underwriting the normative foundations of tributary relations. He concludes that a historical-sociological attention to sociocultural forces uncovers dynamics in non-Western interpolity orders that state-centric models cannot see.

entries.title: The Rise and Fall of Status-Seekers: Commitment, Strategy, and International Political Change in East Asia
entries.venue: Ph.D. dissertation, Department of Political Science, McGill University
entries.summary: Argues that status ascent cannot be explained by a state's strategy alone: whether a status-seeker rises or falls depends on the synchronization between its strategy and the international social structure surrounding it during a period of order transition. Builds the theory from East Asian history rather than from European cases, comparing Korean and Japanese status-seeking across the Ming-Qing transition (1583-1683), the Westphalian transition (1839-1912) and Détente (1969-1979), and offers the resulting framework as a tool for reading contemporary challenges to the liberal order while bridging IR theory with historical and area-studies scholarship.

entries.title: 사대의 국제정치이론: 일어난 미래로서 병자호란 [International Theory of Serving the Great: 1636 Qing Invasion of Chosŏn as a Future-Passed]
entries.venue: 국제정치논총 [Korean Journal of International Relations]
entries.summary: Argues that sadae (serving the great), the principle governing Ming–Chosŏn relations until the 1636 Qing invasion, contains the seed of a post-sovereign international theory that historians and IR scholars have missed by reading it only within its own context as a specimen of the 'tributary system.' Using Marilyn Strathern's ethnographic moment, Choi treats the anti-accommodation (척화) discourse of 1636 as a 'future-passed' and reconstructs it together with the Neo-Confucian nature/coherence (性卽理) and Eight Steps schemas into a monadological international theory: political units are monads that contain the whole order within themselves, so states become non-sovereign monads cultivating attunement to the coherence of their overall relational configuration. The reconstruction is offered as an alternative field of IR knowledge production and a contribution to the discipline's pluralization.

entries.title: 'Chinese' hegemony from a Korean shi perspective: aretocracy in the early modern East Asia
entries.venue: International Relations of the Asia-Pacific
entries.summary: Argues that pre-modern 'Chinese' hegemony was not the unilateral normative projection of the Chinese state but a reciprocal rule of virtue — aretocracy — driven by the transnational sociocultural elite, the shi. Chinese and non-Chinese shi co-produced the hegemonic order out of a shared civilizational heritage, and within it authority was legitimate only for those who demonstrated excellence in civil virtues; the Ming and Chosŏn shi built a tradition of envoy-poetry exchange as the medium of that co-construction. Choi draws the normative implication that world-order making can rest on cultivated ethos rather than on state power alone.

entries.title: Virtue Rules: The Evolution of the Virtue of State in East Asian International Orders
entries.venue: Johns Hopkins University (Ph.D. dissertation, Department of Political Science)
entries.summary: Argues that the 'virtue of state' is simultaneously a crucial form of state power and a constituent of international order: it confers power by making a state the leader in cultivating collective attunement among states, and it orders them by finely attuning them to social and natural forces — which especially advantages weak states in a hegemonic order, since virtue can be cultivated without material resources. States cultivate virtue through a dialectic of performance and evaluation within an 'evaluative community,' which requires the state to possess a fictional moral personhood. Choi traces three such fictions — the monadic, the sovereign and the liberal state — showing that the moral fiction of state arose separately in Warring States China and early modern Europe before the two traditions merged in nineteenth-century East Asia, where scholars translated legal sovereignty into a state virtue to cope with imperialism, and that liberal internationalism functions as a further state fiction through which the South Korean public and liberal networks cultivate liberal virtue. The payoff is an alternative conception of state agency: a flexible repertoire of virtues in place of the ineffectual pursuit of sovereignty.

entries.title: 프랑코 통치 하 스페인의 모로코 영토 협상: 존재론적 안보로서 스페인의 제국적 정체성 [The Negotiation Surrounding Morocco by Spain under Franco's Rule: Ontological Security and Spain's Imperial Identity]
entries.venue: 국제정치논총 [Korean Journal of International Relations / KJIR], Korean Association of International Studies
entries.summary: Argues that Franco's insistence on annexing French Morocco during his 1940 bargaining with Hitler and Mussolini cannot be explained by material or strategic interest: a Spain devastated by the civil war stood to gain far more by entering the war on Germany's terms, and Hitler, who was courting Vichy France, could not concede Morocco. Reading the impasse through ontological security, the article contends that Morocco functioned as the indispensable symbol through which a fallen empire could restore biographical continuity with its imperial self, so Franco preferred deadlock and non-belligerence to surrendering it. The case is used to show that identity interests, and the organizing principle of inter-imperial Europe from which Spain had been disengaged, can override calculable physical gain.

entries.title: 프랑코 통치 하 스페인의 제국 정체성과 모로코 영토외교(1940): 존재론적 안보 접근 [Imperial Identity of Spain under Franco's Rule and Moroccan Territorial Diplomacy (1940): An Ontological Security Approach]
entries.venue: MA thesis, Graduate School, Seoul National University — Division of Political Science and International Relations, Major in Diplomacy (서울대학교 대학원 정치외교학부 외교학전공)
entries.summary: Asks why Franco sought to expand the Spanish protectorate into French Morocco despite Spain's ruinous political and economic condition immediately after the civil war. Argues that the answer lies in an imperial identity that must be read against the organizing principle of empires in Europe rather than reduced to Franco's personal ambition, reconstructing Spain's self-narrative as a fallen empire disengaged from inter-imperial norms of sovereignty. Concludes that the imperial bid failed because competing international organizing principles collided — above all as U.S.-centred arrangements displaced the older European imperial framework. This thesis is the basis of the co-authored 2019 국제정치논총 article.

themes.title: Ontological Complexity and the Encounter with Others
themes.blurb: Pushes past multiculturalism — the assumption that one reality is merely represented in many idioms — to argue that participants in a single order can inhabit genuinely different lived worlds, as the Chosŏn envoys and the Panchen Lama did at Qianlong's birthday. The same move is then turned on the present: on how a researcher must be undone by an infinitely distant Other, on U.S.–China rivalry as an encounter of ontological others, and on a divided peninsula read as a pre-individual field rather than two finished states.

entries.title: Ontological Complexity of Interpolity Orders: The Encounter between Chosŏn and Tibet in Qing
entries.venue: European Journal of International Relations
entries.summary: Reframes the Qing order as ontologically complex rather than merely culturally diverse: existing multiculturalist accounts assume one imperial reality represented in many idioms, whereas the authors argue that peripheral participants inhabited genuinely different lived worlds. Reading Pak Chiwŏn's travelogue against Tibetan records of the Chosŏn envoys' meeting with the Panchen Lama at Qianlong's birthday ceremony, they show the Confucian envoys experienced the Lama as subhuman while the Lama experienced them as ignorant lay beings; observing this dissonance, Pak criticized the Qing court's appropriation of peripheral ontologies and proposed inhabiting other ontologies to foreground the pluriverse. The article argues an ontological approach can reconceptualize interpolity order generally, beyond the Qing case.

entries.title: 객관, 주체, 그리고 타자의 국제정치학: 타자 만남의 목표, 이론, 방법 [International Relations of Encountering the Other: Aim, Theory, and Methodology]
entries.venue: 국제정치논총 [Korean Journal of International Relations]
entries.summary: Argues that IR's metatheoretical debate has offered only two kinds of knowledge — objective knowledge won by bracketing the knowing subject, and practical or self-knowledge reflecting a positioned subjectivity — and that both miss the discipline's latent core problem, the existential logic of encountering alterity. Drawing on Levinas's philosophy of the Other, the ontological turn, and hermeneutic distanciation, Choi proposes an IR built around confrontation with an infinitely distant Other that deconstructs and then reconstructs the researcher's theoretical frame and lived experience, and reconfigures geopolitical questions from that standpoint.

entries.authors: 하영선, 권민주, 정연 (Young-Sun Ha, Minju Kwon and Yan Zheng)
entries.title: 열하의 국제정치: 청, 티베트, 조선 [International Politics of Rehe: Qing, Tibet, and Chosŏn]
entries.venue: 하영선·이헌미 편 [Young-Sun Ha and Hunmi Lee (eds.)], 사행의 국제정치: 16-19세기 조천·연행록 분석 [International Politics of Tributary Envoys: An Analysis of Chocheonnok and Yeonhaengnok, 16th-19th Centuries], Seoul: Asiatic Research Institute, Korea University
entries.summary: An early Korean-language study of the Rehe (Jehol) encounter among Qing, Tibetan, and Chosŏn actors, read through Chosŏn envoy travel records -- the empirical terrain Kwon later develops with Inho Choi into the 2025 EJIR argument about ontological complexity in the Qing order. NOTE: verified only from Kwon's own CV; the chapter title given here is a back-translation of the CV's romanized entry and the volume's table of contents could not be independently retrieved, so exact chapter title and pagination should be checked against the printed book.

themes.title: Race, Gender, and the Standards of Civilization
themes.blurb: The collective's second research module, taken at the level where hierarchy is actually lived: bobbed hair in colonial Korean magazines, Japan's trade of naval tonnage for civilizational standing after the racial equality proposal failed, a Geneva Protocol article that spares mothers the noose but not the sentence. Read together the papers argue that civilizational and racial standards were co-produced by the people they ranked — colonized women, non-Western elites, fans and survivors — and that agency in these settings takes forms that neither resistance nor complicity describes.

entries.title: All but the Death Penalty: Incomplete Protection for Civilian Internee Mothers
entries.venue: Feminist Legal Studies
entries.summary: Argues that unrecognized gender bias is built into the codification of international humanitarian law itself. Focusing on Article 76(3) of the 1977 Additional Protocol I, which forbids executing pregnant women and mothers of dependent children who are interned but still permits the death sentence to be pronounced against them, Kwon draws on the theory of benevolent sexism to contend that this 'preferential protection' encodes an essentialist picture of women as weak protectees by default. She further argues such benevolent protection predictably lapses once it collides with state interests in retaining discretion over women whose conduct exceeds traditional gender roles.

entries.title: Short-Haired Modern Girls: Colonial Korean Women's Fashion as the Standards of Civilization
entries.venue: European Journal of International Relations
entries.summary: Argues that gendered actors -- above all colonized women -- actively constituted the interwar standard of civilization rather than merely being measured against it, and that everyday politics of fashion was a site where that standard was contested. Reading debates over women's short hair in colonial Korean magazines and newspapers, Kwon shows that the so-called Modern Girls interpreted and practiced civilizational standards under three stacked hierarchies at once (non-Western polity, colonized nation, patriarchal society), defending bobbed hair as economically efficient, hygienic, aesthetically valuable, and emancipatory while being ceaselessly degraded for failing to embody 'genuine' modernity. The article thereby recasts the plurality of modernity through women's fashioned bodies and pushes Global IR to credit agency in non-Western, non-imperial societies.

entries.title: Cohabitation with Criminals: Civilian Women's Everyday Cooperation with Mexican Drug Cartels
entries.venue: International Feminist Journal of Politics
entries.summary: Argues that scholarship on women under narco-violence has been trapped between two extremes -- active resistance or direct cartel participation -- while most civilian women in fact act somewhere in between. Drawing on 37 semi-structured interviews in Jalisco, the authors develop the concept of 'everyday cooperation' and sort women's cohabitation with cartels into three modes: keeping silent, pursuing benefits, and idealizing narco-culture. They contend that although these actions are shaped by the normalization of violence in local communities, women strategize them through social learning, so that cooperation should be read as a form of civilian agency rather than passivity.

entries.title: Japan's Status-Driven Restraint Despite Racial Humiliation, 1921–1936
entries.venue: The Journal of American-East Asian Relations (Brill)
entries.summary: Against status-and-race theories that predict racial humiliation will push a rising power toward revisionism, Oh asks why Japan accepted an inferior naval ratio and stayed committed to the Washington naval system from 1921 to 1930 despite the 1919 rejection of its racial equality proposal and the 1924 Japanese Exclusion Act. He argues, in a constructivist-realist register, that Japan's orthodox foreign policy idea prioritized its higher *civilizational* status relative to both the Western powers and the rest of East Asia, producing an elite consensus among civilian and military leaders that accepted a trade-off of reduced military capability for increased status. Restraint therefore persisted until that elite consensus collapsed and the political-economic shock of the Showa Depression defeated social expectations in the early 1930s — showing that racial humiliation alone does not time revisionism.

entries.title: Sarcasm or Sexism? Media Framing of Duterte's Misogynistic Speeches
entries.venue: Asian Journal of Women's Studies
entries.summary: Shows that Philippine news media systematically defused Rodrigo Duterte's misogynistic public speech rather than reporting it as abuse. Through qualitative content analysis of 265 reports from seven domestic outlets covering three incidents (fantasizing about raping an Australian missionary, threatening to shoot female rebel soldiers in the vagina, and denying women's fitness for the presidency), the authors find pervasive underreporting and three recurring frames: treating the speeches as feminist rather than human rights issues, as sarcastic jokes rather than genuine misogyny, and as individual deviance rather than structural sexism. The article argues that studies of media representation of leaders' misogyny must be recast for non-Western local contexts.

entries.title: Relatively Unworthy Victims? Middle-Aged Women as Rape Survivors
entries.venue: Violence Against Women
entries.summary: Demonstrates through an online survey experiment in China that the age of a rape survivor changes how seriously the public treats the crime: respondents judged rape as less serious, and requested shorter sentences, when the survivor was a middle-aged woman than when she was younger, older, or of unstated age. The authors argue that Chinese moral codes around chastity and respect for elders generate stronger emotional response on behalf of younger and older survivors, leaving middle-aged women as comparatively 'unworthy' victims, and thereby extend rape-perception research to an age group it has largely ignored.

themes.title: International Law, Institutions, and Contested Legitimacy
themes.blurb: Follows legitimacy as something armed groups, states and humanitarian gatekeepers must continually manufacture before domestic and international audiences — rebels signing UN action plans on child soldiers, a vigilante militia in Borno, the ICRC deciding whether to break its own confidentiality, five Northeast Asian claimants using the UN Charter against one another. It supplies the collective's institutional and legal register, showing that formal international machinery runs on recognition contests rather than on compliance alone.

entries.summary: Examines how the content of United Nations mission mandates -- specifically their rule-of-law components -- shapes foreign direct investment into host states, arguing that peace operations affect investor behaviour through the legal-institutional provisions they carry rather than through the mere presence of peacekeepers.
