NOTE: listed on her research page but not on the CV version obtained; unpublished, no draft publicly circulated.

entries.title: Why in the Upper Nile but Not in West Africa?: Britain's Atypical Preventive War Motivation, the Contagion Effect, and the Fashoda Crisis Revisited, 1882-1898
entries.venue: Manuscript under review — Revise & Resubmit at Cambridge Review of International Affairs
entries.summary: Applying his contagion-effect framework to Anglo-French colonial rivalry, Oh asks why Britain was willing to risk war over the Upper Nile at Fashoda in 1898 while tolerating comparable French encroachment in West Africa. He argues that Britain's preventive war motivation was activated selectively — not by aggregate power shifts but by expectations that a French position on the Upper Nile would propagate along the first line of imperial maritime defense. Status per Oh's July 2026 CV: R&R at Cambridge Review of International Affairs.

entries.title: Explaining the Absence of War during the U.S.–China Naval Power Transition, 2012–2025: Power Projection, Contagion Expectations, and Alignment Opportunity
entries.venue: Manuscript in revision
entries.summary: Oh takes the puzzle of peace: China quantitatively overtook the United States in combat hull count without war, contrary to what power-transition pessimism would predict. He argues the absence of war follows from his two conditions — Washington's expectations about the contagion effect of Chinese power projection on its first line of naval defense have not yet been triggered in a way that activates preventive motivation, while alignment opportunity in the Indo-Pacific has remained open to the United States. Earlier versions were presented at APSA 2024 under the title 'Explaining the Absence of a War over China's Quantitative Naval Overtake, 2008-2024.'

entries.title: Neither a Liar nor a Peacemaker: The First Line of Naval Defense and Roosevelt's Expectations about the Contagion Effect in the Asia-Pacific, 1934-1941
entries.venue: Manuscript in revision
entries.summary: Intervening in the long-running historiographical fight over whether Franklin D. Roosevelt deceived the American public into war or genuinely sought peace, Oh argues that FDR was neither: his shifting Asia-Pacific policy tracked his evolving expectations about the contagion effect of Japanese expansion on the American first line of naval defense. The paper reframes the provocation-versus-restraint debate as a question about how a leading sea power draws and redraws its defense perimeter.

entries.title: A Logic of North Korea's Nuclear Foreign Policy and the Security-Legitimacy Dilemma, 1994-2019
entries.venue: Manuscript in revision
entries.summary: Oh argues that North Korean nuclear concessions have followed a specifiable logic rather than caprice: they occurred when accumulated domestic economic pressure eroded regime legitimacy at the same moment that a credible U.S. commitment to political normalization was on offer, so that normalization could function as a security asset substituting for nuclear deterrence. When U.S. credibility collapsed, Pyongyang reverted to weapons development despite economic hardship — evidence that security concerns dominate economic pressure. Earlier versions circulated as 'A Causal Logic of Authoritarian Nuclear Concession' (APSA 2022, ISA 2021).

entries.title: Beyond Decent Peace: Toward Effective Peace in an Era of Systemic Transformation
entries.venue: Manuscript in revision
entries.summary: Co-authored with Inho Choi, this paper argues that the prevailing normative standard of a 'decent peace' is inadequate to an era of systemic transformation, and proposes 'effective peace' as an alternative criterion oriented to whether a settlement can actually hold under conditions of order transition. Listed among manuscripts in revision on Oh's July 2026 CV.

entries.title: Modern Construction of Ancient Nations: The Role of 'Unification' in the Historical Development of East Asian Nations
entries.venue: Paper presented at the ISA Annual Convention 2026, Columbus, OH — Panel SB052, 'Rethinking Historical East Asia: Beyond Presentism, State-Centrism, and Essentialism' (Historical International Relations section; discussant Daniel M. Green, University of Delaware; co-panelists Seo-Hyun Park and Jaeyoung Kim)
entries.summary: Unpublished conference paper; ISA does not publish abstracts in the program PDF, so this description is inferred from the title and from the panel's stated remit rather than from an abstract. The paper treats 'unification' as a retrospective political construct rather than a natural endpoint of national history, arguing that the nations of historical East Asia were made modern by projecting a unified ancient origin backwards — the panel frames this as a corrective to presentism, state-centrism and essentialism in accounts of the region.

entries.title: The Dawn of the Global International Community: Case of Korea in the Second Hague Peace Conference and the League of Nations
entries.venue: Paper presented at the ISA Annual Convention 2026, Columbus, OH — Panel TC094, 'Humanitarian Interventions and Negotiations'
entries.summary: Unpublished conference paper; no abstract is printed in the ISA program, so this description is inferred from the title and from her stated research programme. The paper uses Korea's appeals at the Second Hague Peace Conference (1907) and to the League of Nations as test cases for when and how a putatively 'global' international community came into being, reading Korea's exclusion as constitutive of, rather than incidental to, the universalization of European international society.

entries.title: Connecting the Moving Dots: 'State,' 'Empire,' and False Linguistic Equivalences in Nineteenth-Century East Asia
entries.venue: Paper presented at the ISA Annual Convention 2025 ('Reconnecting International Studies'), Chicago, IL — Panel MA50, 'Historicizing Global IR and Globalizing Historical IR: Interconnected Histories of the Global Order' (Global IR / Historical IR sections; chair Hendrik Spruyt, discussant Young Chul Cho; co-panelists Inho Choi, Sujin Heo, Jaeyoung Kim, Filippo Costa Buranelli)
entries.summary: Unpublished conference paper; no abstract is printed in the ISA program, so this description is inferred from the title and her stated research programme. The paper argues that nineteenth-century translations equating East Asian political vocabulary with European 'state' and 'empire' created false linguistic equivalences, and that IR's inherited categories therefore mis-describe the polities they claim to cover — a case for reading the global order through the movement and mistranslation of concepts rather than through fixed units.

entries.title: 'Empire' with a Lowercase 'E': the Formation of Modern Concept of 'Empire' from the Case of China, Vietnam, Korea, and Tibet
entries.venue: Paper presented at the ISA Annual Convention 2025, Chicago, IL — Panel WA20, 'Explorers, Empires and World Making in the History of International Relations' (Historical IR / Global IR sections; chair Kerry Goettlich)
entries.summary: Unpublished conference paper; no abstract is printed in the ISA program, so this description is inferred from the title and her stated research programme. Working across China, Vietnam, Korea and Tibet, the paper argues that the modern generic concept of 'empire' — empire with a lowercase 'e', a type of polity rather than the name of one — was formed out of these encounters, so that the analytic category IR uses to describe East Asia was itself partly produced there.

entries.title: Emperor at Home, King Abroad: Coexistence of Multiple Emperors in Historical East Asia
entries.venue: Paper presented at the ISA Annual Convention 2024, San Francisco, CA — Panel SC32, 'International Relations and Historical Sociology in East Asia' (Historical IR / International Political Sociology sections; discussant Andrew Phillips; co-panelists Inho Choi, Naosuke Mukoyama, Minju Kwon, Maria Adele Carrai). Subsequently presented at the 2025 USC Graduate Conference in Korean Studies (Panel 1, 'Sinitic Heritages in Korea and Beyond', 7 Feb 2025) and at the ANU Coral Bell School GRADNAS seminar (8 May 2025).
entries.summary: Unpublished conference paper. Per the ANU seminar flyer describing this talk, Roh 'reconsiders the "state vs empire" and "anarchy vs hierarchy" dichotomies by revisiting the concept of the "emperor" in historical East Asia': taking seriously that several rulers styled themselves emperor at home while presenting as kings abroad, she argues that historical East Asia sustained multiple simultaneous emperorships, which neither the anarchy-of-equal-states model nor a single-hierarchy tributary model can accommodate.

entries.title: China's Complex Grand Strategy Tradition: A Pragmatist Interpretation
entries.venue: Working paper (listed on the author's site under Works in Progress)
entries.summary: Argues against both the Confucian-moral-hierarchy and the realist/imperialist readings of Chinese strategy, contending that Chinese grand strategy draws on a millennia-long repertoire of at least five modes — ritual ordering, cherishing men from afar, loose-rein governance, military punishment, and peaceful alignment — each keyed to a different power configuration from dominance to parity. Choi highlights the overlooked practice of peaceful alignment, by which Chinese dynasties kept stable relations with stronger rivals such as the Liao, as the closest analogue to the PRC's preoccupation with managing the United States, and adopts a pragmatist framework in which historical legacies are adaptively reinterpreted rather than simply repeated.

entries.title: US-China Strategy for the Rest: Toward Planetary Coevolution
entries.venue: Working paper (listed on the author's site under Works in Progress)
entries.summary: Argues that leaving the U.S.-China relationship to the two protagonists is a formula for global disorder, and that a strategic framework 'for the rest' — above all for neighboring middle powers such as South Korea — is both necessary and feasible. Choi proposes 'planetary coevolution' as a middle-power grand strategy: a long-term project of converting both superpowers and other states into agents whose aim is not competitive victory but the construction of a non-hegemonic, federative security system in which states keep democratic autonomy and self-determination while binding themselves to shared restraining architectures capable of handling risks no single power can manage.

entries.title: The Enemy of My Enemy is Myself: US-China Rivalry as the Encounter of Ontological Others
entries.venue: Working paper (listed on the author's site under Works in Progress)
entries.summary: Argues that stably managing the U.S.-China rivalry requires rethinking it as an encounter between ontological others — actors whose divergent lived realities can fundamentally challenge and transform each other's self-understanding — a possibility mainstream great-power-competition theory ignores and critical IR has barely applied to rivalry. Using the ontological turn in anthropology and Ricoeur's hermeneutics of distanciation, Choi contends that each side must concretely experience itself as its enemy's enemy, a rival threatening not only physical security but ontological integrity; that realization would blunt both powers' self-righteous normative claims and induce prudence.

entries.title: Eurocentrism as Self-Empowerment: A Genealogy of Korean Self-Determination in the Modern International Order
entries.venue: Working paper (listed on the author's site under Works in Progress)
entries.summary: Reconceptualizes Eurocentrism as not only an oppressive epistemic structure, as Said, Chakrabarty and Spivak emphasize, but also a historically productive resource for non-Western national self-fashioning. Choi argues that from the late nineteenth century Korean elites deliberately adopted European political and intellectual standards as a strategy of self-strengthening (自强, chagang) against Western and Japanese imperial pressure, yet read those standards through an indigenous tradition of moral self-cultivation — turning Eurocentrism into a means of renewing rather than erasing their own heritage, and enabling modernization, liberation and later integration into the U.S.-led order without surrendering cultural agency.

entries.title: Invention of Another State in Warring States China: Toward a Complex History of the State and International Order
entries.venue: Working paper (listed on the author's site under Works in Progress)
entries.summary: Argues that Warring States Chinese thinkers invented a non-European genealogy of the modern state: like its European counterpart it was an impersonal entity grounded in secular political knowledge and serving as both reference and goal of governing a population, but it diverged in being embedded within the universal moral order of tianxia rather than in a system of multiple sovereign states. Choi contends that this invention and its later East Asian transformations oblige scholars of European state formation, of the nineteenth-century globalization of the international order, and of non-Western orders to replace the single-origin narrative with a complex history of multiple state trajectories converging in the nineteenth century.

entries.title: [South Korea's North Korea Policy] ① Toward an Individuation Strategy for the Korean Peninsula: The Abandonment of North Korea's Security-Legitimacy Dilemma and the Long-Term Korean Strategy toward North Korea
entries.venue: Global NK Special Report, East Asia Institute
entries.summary: Oh argues that the 'security-legitimacy dilemma' logic that once made North Korean nuclear concessions possible was abandoned after the collapse of the Hanoi summit — Pyongyang codified nuclear status in law (2022), adopted a hostile two-state doctrine (2023), and gave up on unification. Drawing on Chaesung Chun's notion of incomplete sovereignty and on Gilbert Simondon's philosophy of individuation, he recasts the peninsula not as two completed sovereign states but as a single 'pre-individual field' charged with unresolved potential energy. Rather than positing one unification outcome and imposing a form on it, he proposes a 'Korean Peninsula Individuation Strategy': cultivating in advance the conditions for a bifurcation favorable to South Korea across four scenarios (frozen metastability, gradual transduction, bifurcated coexistence, forced individuation), while warning that premature crystallization risks regime-extinction dynamics. Published in both English and Korean.

entries.title: The U.S. Navy's FY2027 Shipbuilding Plan and the Korea–U.S. Shipbuilding Partnership (KUSPI): Institutionalizing Allied Industrial Capacity in the Indo-Pacific and Korea's Proactive Shaping
entries.venue: Global NK Commentary, East Asia Institute
entries.summary: Reading the Korea-U.S. Shipbuilding Partnership Initiative signed on 8 May against the U.S. Navy's FY2027 shipbuilding plan, Oh argues that the 'Bridge Strategy' announced in the February Maritime Action Plan has now been operationalized, and that KUSPI is the first bilateral institutionalization of that strategy at the level of an Indo-Pacific alliance. He urges Seoul not to accept KUSPI as a mere vehicle for inbound investment into the United States but to define it actively as the Indo-Pacific demonstration case for institutionalizing 'allied industrial capacity,' while keeping it coherent with an integrated extended deterrence posture that answers the nuclearization of the North Korean navy. Published in English and Korean.

entries.title: New Spheres of Conflicting Orders: A Lack of Consensus Promises Confusion and Competition
entries.venue: Council of Councils Global Memo — 'The World Reorders: The Complications of a Return to Spheres of Influence,' Council on Foreign Relations
entries.summary: Chun and Oh contend that describing the present shift as a return to spheres of influence is misleading; what is emerging is 'a far more unstable hybrid order, in which different organizing principles coexist and collide.' They identify a core contradiction in U.S. strategy — treating the Western Hemisphere as an American sphere while refusing to concede a Chinese sphere in the Indo-Pacific — which, absent great-power consensus, generates friction and miscalculation. For South Korea and other middle powers, they argue, fragmentation is a greater danger than any single sphere, so the response should be to work with like-minded partners to keep open a space for cooperation, law, inclusiveness, and sovereign equality rather than accept regionalized power systems.

entries.authors: Boris Ruge, Sophie Larder, Alex Bristow, Inhwan Oh, Akira Igata, and David Capie
entries.title: New research hub assesses shared security challenges in the Indo-Pacific and Euro-Atlantic: A view from South Korea
entries.venue: The Strategist, Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI)
entries.summary: In this multi-author launch piece for the Indo-Pacific and Euro-Atlantic Hub for Shared Security Challenges, Oh contributes the South Korean view, arguing that the present moment is neither a new Cold War nor simple multipolarity but an 'unstable hybrid order' in which competing organizing principles asserted by the United States, China, and Russia remain unresolved. He maintains that NATO-IP4 cooperation should be understood as practical partnership among middle powers — 'not about Japan entering NATO, nor about creating an Asian NATO' — a framing that both counters disinformation and enables collective efforts to reshape order through cooperation on security, defense, technology, and standards.

entries.title: Trump's Golden Fleet Initiative, MASGA, and the ICE Pact
entries.venue: Global NK Commentary, East Asia Institute
entries.summary: Oh assesses three linked Trump-administration responses to the U.S.-China naval shift — the Golden Fleet plan for 20-25 next-generation 30,000-40,000-ton destroyers plus frigates, Korean shipbuilders' bid for a larger role through the Philadelphia Shipyard under MASGA, and the unprecedented presidential waiver letting Finland build U.S. Arctic icebreakers under the ICE Pact. He argues that the practical obstacles to Korean participation are legal and structural (U.S. labor costs, skilled-labor shortage, component supply chains, the Buy American Act) rather than technical, and concludes that Seoul's decisive asset is sustained political trust with Washington aligned to the trajectory of the naval power transition — the condition for advancing both MASGA and a Korean nuclear-powered submarine program. Published in English and Korean.

entries.title: The Future of U.S. Maritime Hegemony and Seoul's Strategy: The Role of the U.S. Congress in ROK-U.S. Shipbuilding Cooperation and North Korea Policy
entries.venue: Global NK Commentary, East Asia Institute
entries.summary: Oh argues that ROK-U.S. shipbuilding cooperation is bounded less by industrial capacity than by U.S. legislation governing naval buildup and the domestic shipbuilding industry, and that these are congressional rather than executive constraints. He therefore contends that a comprehensive diplomatic approach aimed at the U.S. Congress is imperative, and that multifaceted congressional engagement would let Seoul advance shipbuilding cooperation while simultaneously aligning long-term Korean and American positions on North Korea policy and the role of U.S. Forces Korea. Published in English and Korean.

entries.authors: Yang Gyu Kim and Inhwan Oh (김양규·오인환)
entries.title: 한국인의 한미일-북중러 블록화 인식과 핵무장 지지 여론 분석: 2025 EAI 동아시아 인식조사 결과 분석 [South Koreans' Perceptions of Blocs between ROK-US-Japan and DPRK-China-Russia and Support for Nuclear Armament: 2025 EAI Public Opinion Survey]
entries.venue: EAI Issue Briefing, East Asia Institute
entries.summary: Using a 1,509-person web panel surveyed on 4-5 June 2025, immediately after the presidential election, Kim and Oh argue that South Korean support for indigenous nuclear armament — at a record 75.1 percent, up from 71.4 percent in 2024 — is being driven less by direct North Korean threat perception (which fell from 56.3 percent in 2023 to 33.2 percent in 2025) than by anxiety about bloc formation. Regression results show that support for ROK-U.S.-Japan security cooperation and the expectation that North Korea will align ever more tightly with China and Russia both independently and significantly predict nuclear support, even as optimism about inter-Korean relations rises. They recommend that the incoming government adopt more sophisticated policy language on U.S.-China competition rather than rhetoric that stimulates the nuclear armament discourse.

entries.title: U.S.-China Naval Power Transition, the First Line of Naval Defense, and the Korean Peninsula
entries.venue: Global NK Commentary, East Asia Institute
entries.summary: Oh reads the Trump administration's April 2025 executive order 'Restoring America's Maritime Dominance' and its Maritime Action Plan as a watershed acknowledgement, at the level of grand strategy, that the United States faces a structural naval shift. He argues that although the U.S. Navy retains qualitative superiority in tonnage, carriers, and nuclear submarines, China's shipbuilding output (53.3 percent of the global market against the U.S. 0.1 percent) constitutes a structural challenge without post-Cold War precedent — and that China's naval modernization itself already functions as a form of structural balancing, making the old puzzle of 'why no balancing against U.S. primacy' largely moot. He then applies his first-line-of-naval-defense framework historically (Palmerston, Salisbury, Roosevelt) to argue that how Washington redraws its Indo-Pacific defense line through 2050 will determine regional stability, and that Seoul — facing simultaneously the naval transition and North Korea's sea-based nuclear modernization — must proactively shape a role through defense-industrial cooperation and a more integrated extended deterrence posture. Published in English and Korean.

entries.title: The United Nations in the Indo-Pacific Era and Competition for Legitimacy in East Asia
entries.venue: Global NK Zoom & Connect (Research Reviews series), East Asia Institute, 29 August 2022
entries.summary: An English-language research review, translated and published by the East Asia Institute, condensing Kwon's Korean-language article with the analytic weight shifted onto North Korea. It argues that because Northeast Asian states are 'incomplete' sovereigns on the modern Western template, they compete for legitimacy inside the UN using the Charter as a symbolic resource, and it presses the point that China's Charter-based insistence on non-interference means its five principles for a peaceful Korean peninsula deserve close scrutiny. NOTE: the live Global NK URL now returns 404; full text confirmed only via the Internet Archive capture.

entries.title: Review of Divergent Worlds: What the Ancient Mediterranean and Indian Ocean Can Tell Us About the Future of International Order, by Amitav Acharya and Manjeet S. Pardesi
entries.venue: Contemporary Southeast Asia (ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute)
entries.summary: Review of Acharya and Pardesi's comparative-historical case that the ancient Mediterranean and Indian Ocean generated fundamentally different kinds of international order, and that multiple world orders can coexist without a single hegemon to hold them together — a claim squarely in the Global IR register Kim's own work occupies. NOTE: the review text itself sits behind the ISEAS paywall and was not read; the citation, the reviewer attribution and the issue's contents were confirmed from the ISEAS table of contents and from Kim's June 2026 CV, which supplies the page range.

entries.title: 한국인과 국제안 [Koreans and the International Eye] — review of 김도민, 『냉전의 진영 너머로: 남북한의 중립·비동맹·제3세계 외교(1948~1976)』 (역사비평사, 2025, 568 pp.)
entries.venue: 인문논총 (Journal of Humanities), Institute of Humanities, Seoul National University
entries.summary: Extended review of Kim Do-min's monograph on North and South Korean diplomacy toward neutral states, non-alignment and the Third World, assessing what a two-Koreas account of Cold War diplomacy beyond the blocs contributes to the history of how Koreans came to see the international.

entries.authors: 김도민, 옥창준, 장문석, 허은, 문미라 (Kim Do-min, Chang Joon Ok, Jang Moon-seok, Heo Eun, Moon Mi-ra)
entries.title: '한반도 냉전사' 쓰기의 도전과 과제 — 김도민, 『냉전의 진영 너머로: 남북한의 중립·비동맹·제3세계 외교(1948~1976)』 (역사비평사, 2025) [The Challenges and Tasks of Writing a 'Cold War History of the Korean Peninsula']
entries.venue: 역사문제연구 (Critical Studies on Modern Korean History)
entries.summary: A multi-author review symposium in which Ok is one of the discussants, debating what it would take to write a Cold War history of the Korean peninsula that holds both Koreas and the Third World in a single frame rather than reproducing bloc-centred narratives.

entries.title: 그래픽노블로 본 국제법의 역사 — 올리비에 코르텐·피에르 클랭 지음, 제라르 브도레 그림, 『국제법의 역사: 살라망카에서 관타나모까지』 [International Law as Iconotext: Visualizing Its Global History through a Graphic Novel]
entries.venue: 서양사연구 (The Journal of Western History)
entries.summary: Reviews the Corten–Klein–Bédorez graphic history of international law as an 'iconotext,' arguing that the visual form does specific analytical work in narrating international law's global history from Salamanca to Guantánamo — a history in which the discipline's universal claims and its imperial uses are drawn on the same page.

entries.title: 오지의 지질학자가 남긴 연구 기록 [The Research Record Left by a Geologist of the Hinterland] — review of 『김용구 연구 회고록』
entries.venue: 서울리뷰오브북스 (Seoul Review of Books), no. 18 (Summer 2025), Aleph
entries.summary: Reviews the research memoir of the international-relations scholar Kim Yong-koo, casting him as a geologist rather than a geographer of world politics — someone who, working from the 'hinterland' of the Korean peninsula, combined comparative civilization with conceptual history to dig beneath the surface features of international order.

entries.title: 과거로 미래 만들기 [Making the Future out of the Past] — review of 백영서, 『동아시아 담론의 계보와 미래: 대안체제의 길』 (나남출판, 2022)
entries.venue: 아시아리뷰 (Asia Review), Seoul National University Asia Center
entries.summary: Review of Baek Young-seo's genealogy of East Asian discourse, engaging Baek's claim that the East Asia discourse can supply a path toward an alternative regional system.

entries.title: 글로벌 세미-노스에서 글로벌 사우스 읽기 [Reading the Global South from the Global Semi-North] — review of 김태균, 『반둥 이후: 글로벌 사우스의 국제정치사회학』 (진인진, 2023)
entries.venue: 황해문화 (Hwanghae Review), Saeol Cultural Foundation
entries.summary: Reviews Kim Taekyoon's international political sociology of the Global South, and uses the review to press the question of where South Korea — a 'global semi-North' — stands when it reads and writes about the Global South.

entries.title: 사상사로 본 한국 현대사 [Intellectual History of Korean Contemporary History] — review of 홍정완, 『한국 사회과학의 기원: 이데올로기와 근대화의 이론 체계』 (역사비평사, 2021)
entries.venue: 인문논총 (Journal of Humanities), Institute of Humanities, Seoul National University
entries.summary: Review essay on Hong Jeong-wan's history of the origins of Korean social science, assessing the claim that ideology and modernization theory jointly structured the postwar Korean academy and situating that argument against Ok's own account of Cold War knowledge reconstruction.

entries.title: Can states trust each other? (review article on Peter Schröder, Trust in Early Modern International Political Thought, 1598-1713, Cambridge University Press, 2017)
entries.venue: History of European Ideas
entries.summary: Reviews Schröder's account of trust across three seventeenth-century traditions - reason of state and balance of power, natural jurisprudence and the law of nations, and perpetual peace projects - and presses a critical objection: the book's own evidence suggests that trust was not in fact foundational to early modern international political thought. Tracing the argument from Gentili's theory of sovereignty through the European peace proposals, the reviewers contend that sovereignty, rather than trust, was the organising problem of these debates.

entries.title: Reflecting a "Pluralist Turn" in International Relations (review of Yong-Soo Eun, Pluralism and Engagement in the Discipline of International Relations, Palgrave Macmillan, 2016)
entries.venue: International Studies Review
entries.summary: Reads Eun's book as arguing for an engaged, dialogical pluralism rather than a unifying synthesis of IR approaches, and highlights its notion of 'reflective pluralism' - the claim that pluralism carries praxical commitments and that IR scholars must practise self-reflection as organic intellectuals. Assesses the book as a thought-provoking intervention precisely because it addresses positivist and post-positivist audiences at once.

entries.authors: 곽귀병, 김일환, 김채연, 옥창준 (Kwak Kwi-byung, Kim Il-hwan, Kim Chae-yeon and Chang Joon Ok)
entries.title: 평화기획으로 한국전쟁 다시 읽기? [Re-reading the Korean War?: The Panmunjom Regime as a Liberal Peace Project]
entries.venue: 사회와 역사 (Society and History), Korean Social History Association
entries.summary: A four-author critical review essay that interrogates attempts to recast the Korean War and the armistice order at Panmunjom as a liberal 'peace project,' questioning whether the peace-making frame can carry the coercive realities of the armistice regime.

entries.authors: 벤자민 영 (Benjamin R. Young); 고자연, 김도민, 김태경, 류기현, 백원담, 옥창준 (translators)
entries.title: 총, 게릴라 그리고 위대한 지도자 — 북한과 제3세계 관계사 [Guns, Guerillas, and the Great Leader: North Korea and the Third World]
entries.venue: 너머북스 (Nomo Books), 너머의 글로벌 히스토리 14
entries.summary: Co-translation of Benjamin Young's history of how North Korea carved out a niche through three decades of Third World diplomacy from the 1950s to the 1980s — a companion to Ok's own research on the Pyongyang Declarations and North Korea's imaginative geography.

entries.venue: Oxford University Press (Korean edition)

entries.venue: 너머북스 (Nomo Books)

entries.venue: 에코리브르 (Ecolivres)
entries.summary: Co-translation of Westad's Bancroft Prize-winning reinterpretation of the Cold War as a contest fought out through interventions in the Third World — the work that anchors Ok's own effort to decentre the Cold War from Washington and Moscow.

entries.authors: 백원담, 오드 아르네 웨스타 (dialogue participants); 옥창준 (translator)
entries.title: 북핵, 냉전, 동아시아, 세계 — 냉전과 탈냉전, 아시아의 역사적 오늘을 살아가는 방법 [North Korean Nuclear Issue, Cold War, East Asia, and the World]

entries.summary: Ok translated this published dialogue between Baik Won-dam and Odd Arne Westad on the North Korean nuclear question, Sino-Korean relations and the state of Cold War historiography — an early instance of the brokering role between global Cold War history and Korean readerships that runs through his translation work.

entries.summary: Ok served as academic supervisor for the Korean edition of this graphic history of international law, and separately published a review essay on it in The Journal of Western History (2026).
